item.title: Shein Was Fast Fashion’s Next Big Thing. Now It’s Fighting for a Second Act.
item.description:
Shein was once one of the most talked-about companies in retail.

It could spot what Generation Z wanted and, within days, turn those trends into $10 mesh dresses and $5 crop tops. Its clothes were so cheap and its churn of new styles was so relentless that #Sheinhaul became a phenomenon on TikTok. Shein overtook bigger rivals like Zara and H&M, started planning an initial public offering and, at one point, was valued at nearly $100 billion.

Now the buzz has faded.

After years of delay, Shein is close to going public — this time at a fraction of its peak valuation. It is searching for new ways to grow after the United States and Europe dismantled tariff exemptions on cheap goods that had helped underpin its low-cost model. Sales have fallen sharply in the United States, its largest market. And the company has offered investors few specifics about where meaningful new growth will come from.

“For a company as hyped as it was for such a long time, the music has seemingly run out,” said Juozas Kaziukenas, an independent e-commerce analyst.

No Chinese fashion brand has been as successful as Shein at going global. And yet the company remains unusually reclusive.

Its founder and chief executive, Sky Xu Yangtian, is so private that until he appeared publicly in February, most of the photographs circulating online purporting to show him were false. Even a senior overseas Shein executive, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak with the media, said he had never met or interacted with Mr. Xu.

Shein declined requests for an interview. The timing and pricing details of its market debut have not been announced, but the company filed a prospectus with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange last month.

Shein has taken pains to distance itself from its Chinese origins. In 2019, it established its headquarters in Singapore and de-registered its original Chinese corporate entity a few years later. The aim was, in part, to navigate Chinese rules governing companies seeking offshore listings and clear a path toward an I.P.O. in New York.

The strategy failed. In the United States, Shein encountered intense, bipartisan scrutiny from lawmakers over its supply chain and labor practices. After abandoning its New York listing effort in 2024, it turned to London, where it faced similar resistance from nongovernmental organizations and other protesters.

That left Hong Kong as the last major viable venue. But after years of delay, analysts say Shein may have missed its moment.

The turn toward Hong Kong has also put Shein in the awkward position of having to re-embrace the Chinese identity it once tried to play down. In China, the company has faced criticism for “blooming in China but bearing fruit abroad” — a phrase suggesting that Shein built its success in the country while redirecting profits overseas.

Then, in February, the famously elusive Mr. Xu suddenly appeared before officials in Guangdong Province.

“Guangdong is Shein’s root,” he declared, announcing that Shein would invest about $1.4 billion over the next three years to build a supply chain hub there.

Chinese media initially covered the speech. Then some articles began disappearing from the internet. Lu Minghe, a veteran journalist, posted a notice showing that Shein had demanded that his public WeChat account remove an article about Mr. Xu’s appearance, citing “infringement.”

Even as Shein recalibrates its relationship with China, a more fundamental problem hangs over any potential listing.

Jianggan Li, founder of Momentum Works, a consultancy that has followed Shein closely, said prospective investors had told him that they sensed little enthusiasm from its founders.

“There hasn’t been any effort to drum up interest,” Mr. Li said. “I don’t feel there’s a strong desire for the management to make the company public, aside from the fact that the investors want to exit.”

Investors are asking how Shein can keep growing.

President Trump’s decision last year to end a policy that had allowed billions of dollars of low-cost imports to enter the United States duty-free dealt a major blow in its single biggest market. In May 2025, Shein began raising prices in the United States. In the first quarter of 2026, U.S. net revenue fell 14.3 percent to $2 billion, the company said.

Europe could pose an even greater challenge. Last month, European authorities announced a 3-euro flat fee on e-commerce parcels that had previously entered duty-free.

Europe accounts for more than a third of Shein’s revenue. In its prospectus, Shein warned that although it was too early to assess the impact of the situation in Europe fully, it “could be generally in line with or exceed the impact observed in the U.S.”

Shein is now trying to convince investors that its future goes beyond ultracheap clothes by selling access to the system it built to design, produce, market and deliver products quickly.

So far, there is little evidence that the supply chain strategy is paying off. Since offering the service as a pilot in 2023, Shein has signed up only about 20 brands. The program generated less than 1 percent of its total net revenue in 2025, according to the company.

Shen Meng, a director at Chanson & Co., an investment banking firm in Beijing, said Shein succeeded in part because it was willing to squeeze its own costs and margins — trade-offs that other brands using its platform may be unwilling to accept.

“It’s hard to see any outstanding advantages in Shein’s transition,” Mr. Shen said.

Shein is also branching out into furniture, cosmetics, pet products and electronics. Nonapparel goods accounted for more than a third of its revenue in the first quarter.

Other analysts are similarly skeptical that Shein has found a second act.

“It’s not clear, other than really cheap, ultrafast fashion, what they’re going to be able to generate,” said Sucharita Kodali, an e-commerce expert at Forrester, a research agency.

Shein’s first act was remarkable.

It was founded in 2012 by Mr. Xu and three colleagues at a marketing firm that helped Chinese exporters sell products online. In 2015, it shortened its name from Sheinside to Shein.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, as online shopping exploded, Shein’s popularity surged. The company saturated the internet with advertisements aimed at young consumers, enticing them with extremely low prices and constantly changing designs.

By 2022, Shein became the world’s biggest online fashion retailer. That year, it was valued at $98.2 billion and backed by a roster of big-name venture capital investors.

The secret was a system built to compress the traditional fashion cycle. Shein used algorithms to track emerging trends, then placed initial orders of a few hundred units to test demand. The model allowed it to introduce approximately 4,700 new apparel styles a day. Zara, by comparison, produces 20,000 a year, according to analysts.

Shein paired that technology with an industrial ecosystem concentrated in Guangdong, where spinners, weavers, seamstresses and small factories could rapidly manufacture orders as small as 100 pieces.

But Shein has struggled to duplicate its Chinese supply chain model in countries such as Turkey and Vietnam, according to Mr. Li of Momentum Works. At the same time, competitors like Temu arrived with even broader product assortments and even lower prices.

Mr. Kaziukenas said he had scoured Shein’s prospectus to find the answer to a question that he’d had for years: “What is the future of Shein?” He added: “I don’t think we got that answer.”

Li You contributed research.

Shein is finally close to getting a public listing after years of delay. It was once the buzziest company in retail but its fortunes have changed dramatically. I reviewed hundreds of pages of corporate documents and spoke to analysts to see where the company stands now and where it’s searching for growth (hint: there aren’t many avenues.)

I know the comments will be filled with virtuous and high minded folks who hate Shein and I'm with you, but as a mom to a teenager who wants to spend her own money there - I think the answer to Shein's downfall is simple. The answer from my teenager's perspective is that prices increased dramatically and she no longer thinks the value is worth the quality.

@Kelly this is interesting. This is what I hear from others too. It does appear that price was the main driving force, and not any brand loyalty.

item.title: Overlooked No More: Patricia Douglas, Who Challenged Hollywood’s Culture of Abuse
item.description:
This article is part of Overlooked, a series of obituaries about remarkable people whose deaths, beginning in 1851, went unreported in The Times.

In May 1937, a 20-year-old extra and dancer named Patricia Douglas was invited to appear in a movie produced by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, the biggest movie studio in Hollywood.

When she showed up on location at the ranch of the producer Hal Roach in Culver City, Calif., she discovered that there was no film shoot. Instead, she later said, she and more than 100 other young women — many of whom were minors — had been summoned to entertain men attending MGM’s annual sales convention.

Douglas later testified in court that during the event, one MGM salesman harassed her, then two men held her down and forced her to drink liquor. Later, she said, the salesman assaulted and raped her in the parking lot.

She reported the attack to prosecutors, pursued a criminal case and sued the studio executives she believed were responsible. She later said MGM mounted a campaign to discredit her, and witnesses mysteriously recanted their earlier statements. A grand jury declined to indict the salesman, her civil suit was dismissed and her story fell out of public memory.

Douglas later said MGM had mounted a campaign to discredit her and had succeeded, and she was blackballed by Hollywood. Years before the #MeToo movement of the late 2010s transformed the way sexual abuse in Hollywood was discussed, Douglas’s story re-emerged because of a curious reporter who had happened upon the case in the course of other research.

“I see her as the Rosa Parks of rape culture,” David Stenn, the reporter, said in an interview. “She stood up against the culture of silence when no one else did.”

Stenn unearthed Douglas’s story in 2003 for a Vanity Fair article, “It Happened One Night at MGM,” and a 2007 film documentary, “Girl 27,” a title taken from the number assigned to Douglas in MGM’s call sheet for the supposed movie shoot — a document he discovered in the Hal Roach archives at the University of Southern California.

Stenn researched the Douglas case for years, digging up grand jury affidavits with sworn testimonies, along with black-and-white film footage of the salesmen arriving at the ranch, where they were welcomed by MGM’s studio chief, Louis B. Mayer. The event was billed as a Wild West show, and the women were given cowgirl costumes to wear.

Karen McNally, the editor of the 2026 book “Women in Hollywood’s Dream Factory: Tales of Inequality, Abuse, and Resistance,” said in an interview that the circumstances surrounding Douglas’s assault were hardly unusual in the 1930s studio system. Young women were routinely brought in to entertain men at industry events, leaving them vulnerable to abuse, she said.

“If you’re repeating the behavior in this manner, which is quite blatant and intentional — that’s a system,” she said.

Patricia Douglas was born Dorothy Shellenberger on March 24, 1917, in Kansas City, Mo., to William Shellenberger, a chauffeur, and Mildred Kritser, who Douglas later estimated had been “married eight times.”

The family moved to Los Angeles in 1920; her parents divorced in 1928. Kritser was a gown designer who “kind of disappeared,” Douglas said, moving into an apartment in Beverly Hills while Dorothy went to live with her grandparents.

At the time, young women from across the country were flocking to Los Angeles, lured by the promise of Hollywood and the opportunities it seemed to offer, especially amid the Great Depression.

“It’s kind of like, ‘Go west, young woman!’ because women have opportunities in Hollywood that they don’t have in other places,” said McNally, who is a professor of American film, television and cultural history at London Metropolitan University. “It’s advertised as something new and wonderful. These young women would have been running around auditioning everywhere.”

At around 14, Dorothy dropped out of school to work as a dancer and changed her name to Patricia Douglas. At 16, she appeared, uncredited, in the 1933 Bert Wheeler-Robert Woolsey comedy “So This Is Africa” and the musical “Gold Diggers of 1933.”

Douglas was in her mid-80s when Stenn tracked her down in Las Vegas, where she was living at the time. With her permission, he recorded their phone conversations for months. He eventually persuaded her to sit for an on-camera interview in 2002.

She told Stenn that the party hosted by MGM was on May 5, 1937, the final night of a four-day convention. A Chicago-based salesman named David Ross approached Douglas on the dance floor. “He kept pestering me to teach him how to truck,” she said. “That was the dance at the time.” He tried every way he could “to get his hands around me,” and eventually she left the dance floor and returned to her table.

There were cases of scotch and champagne, but when Douglas said she didn’t drink alcohol, two salesmen forced her to, by holding her nose and pouring the liquor into her mouth.

She ran to the washroom to vomit, then went out to the parking lot for air. That was when Ross knocked her down, dragged her to his car and raped her, she said.

“The only thing I can remember is this David Ross’s face. It was in my nightmares for many years,” she said in the film documentary. “I could not get him off my mind and what he had done to me. He took my innocence. You can never get that back.”

Her account of the incident became headline news almost immediately after it happened. The Daily Times, a Chicago tabloid paper, ran a full-page headline, “Wild Film Party,” and a sub-headline, “Assault Told by Girl, 17,” for a story that included her name and photo, incorrectly reporting her age as three years younger than she was.

Subsequent news about developments in the case appeared in papers across the country, including The Los Angeles Times, with stories resorting to euphemisms like “ravished” or “outraged” instead of “rape.”

“Rape was literally a four-letter word in the 1930s,” Stenn said. “They wouldn’t print it in the newspapers."

Ross called Douglas’s claims “absurd, ridiculous” and Mayer’s personal attorney defended the salesman in the case, Stenn said.

When the grand jury declined to indict Ross, Douglas refused to let the matter end there. She sued Ross and other studio executives in Los Angeles Superior Court, accusing them of conspiring to “defile, debauch, and seduce” her for “the immoral and sensual gratification of male guests,” according to legal documents. She sought $500,000 in damages — more than $11 million in today’s dollars.

The suit was dismissed in February 1938. The next day, she filed an identical suit in federal court, arguing that the assault had violated her civil rights. It was, Stenn wrote in Vanity Fair, apparently the first time a woman had made rape the basis of a federal civil-rights case. That case, too, was ultimately dismissed because both lawyers failed to show up in court.

In “Girl 27,” Stenn described a cover-up campaign led by executives at MGM, which implicated the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s office and the doctor who had examined Douglas after the attack. Even an eyewitness who had helped her when she emerged from the bushes, crying and bleeding, later denied having seen anything.

“What she did had no real precedent, and she did it in a vacuum when there was no support on any level, no legal protections for women, and such a situation was considered unspeakable,” Stenn said in an interview.

A representative from Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns MGM’s film library from the 1930s, said the company did not have “anyone who can speak on the matter.” The Los Angeles County District Attorney’s office could not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Douglas married and divorced three times and had a daughter from her first marriage. Douglas died on Nov. 11, 2003, in Las Vegas. She was 86.

McNally said that very few cases of harassment and assault in the film industry came to light at the time, unless the woman involved was famous. Although there’s evidence that stars like Lana Turner, Judy Garland, and Shirley Temple faced sexual harassment or assault on the job, those stories often went public long after the incidents occurred.

The fact that Douglas’s case became so widely known was also unusual, McNally said. “Her case was in the press at the time,” she said. “It was headline news, and it was out there at the time, and then just forgotten.”

item.title: Sick of Constant Pings, They’re Sending Texts at the Speed of Carrier Pigeon
item.description:
The carrier pigeon was halfway across the Atlantic Ocean, soaring toward Toronto. Its message, sent from London, would take more than a day to arrive.

But when the letter landed, it was not untied from a spindly leg but rather opened in an app, because this pigeon was digital, not physical.

A lot of time has gone into speeding up human communication, from the telegram to the Pony Express to shouting loudly from a rooftop. Lately, at least two apps have asked: Was a carrier pigeon the pinnacle?

One of the apps exploring this idea is Carrier Pidge, an app that allows users to send messages at the speed of pigeon. Users track their bird on a map as it whips toward its destination.

Like real birds, the digital pigeons have a chance of getting lost or dying — 0.2 percent. Buying a new one within the app will run you 99 cents.

As it turns out, this slower, riskier and costlier version of messaging has wide appeal.

“Some things are better when they’re worse,” said Olivia Macdonald, 27, who uses the app to send messages to her boyfriend. Her texts arrive in minutes — they both live in Manhattan — but the chances of the pigeon disappearing adds intrigue, she said.

“The uncertainty of that, compared to the numbness that we feel receiving so many texts and notifications a day, is something that I just find really attractive about it,” Ms. Macdonald said.

Carrier Pidge, which launched in April, exploded in popularity this month after a post about the app by its developer, Noah Iarrobino, was shared by thousands. After several months with only a couple hundred users, he said, the app now has more than 75,000.

Another app released in April, Roost, which lets users send texts via such animals as including pigeons, snails and penguins, reported that it has reached 650,000 downloads this month.

Both apps have connected with users who are tired of the daily digital grind.

“I was probably inspired by a trend going on in tech — people want to get away from their phones and get outside,” Mr. Iarrobino, 29, said of how the idea came to him. “I thought carrier pigeons were a funny concept, and it would be funny if some of them didn’t make it back.”

Mr. Iarrobino, a software engineer in New York, had developed other apps: One that charges users 99 cents every time they hit snooze on an alarm, another that keeps a leaderboard among users of who touches their phone screen the most in a day.

The first message he sent on Carrier Pidge was to a friend in Chicago — an image of a leotard-clad Danny DeVito from the TV show “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia.” Delivery time: 8 hours and 49 minutes.

The speed of each message varies, with a maximum speed of 110 m.p.h. (Mr. Iarrobino said he researched racing pigeons and found one named Bolt that had been recorded at that pace.)

Roost was designed by Logan Mendelsohn, a 31-year-old product manager. Unlike Carrier Pidge, the app offers over 1,000 animals to choose from, with the speeds to match. (A white Italian snail crawls at a little over one mile an hour, while a barn owl flies at about 20 m.p.h.) It has a “pen pal” feature that lets users meet and message new people.

“My focus is leaning in toward the slow-tech movement, leaning into areas that help people around the world connect,” said Mr. Mendelsohn, whose career has been focused on trust and safety in tech. He said Roost has gotten so big that he is planning to hire employees.

There has been some flag-planting in online comments sections from fans of Roost, who accuse Carrier Pidge of copying the concept. But Mr. Mendelsohn and Mr. Iarrobino said in interviews that neither took ideas from the other and that they have discussed their apps with each other.

Their apps appear to have tapped into a palpable discomfort with screen time and constant communication, and a yearning for an antiquated era.

A 2023 survey conducted by the Harris Poll, in partnership with the Human Flourishing Lab at the Archbridge Institute, found that 80 percent of Gen Z adults — those born after 1997 — were worried that their age group relied too heavily on technology. Fifty-eight percent said that new technologies were more likely to drive people apart than unite them.

“A lot of the digital tools that saturate our attention at the moment were built on the idea that friction is bad,” Cal Newport, a professor of computer science at Georgetown University and the author of “Deep Work,” said in an email.

“The human brain cannot function well in a friction-free world,” he said. “Too much information coming at us too fast overwhelms our ability to switch our attention.”

By reintroducing friction through apps like Carrier Pidge and Roost, Mr. Newport said, messages can be thoughtful and given the attention they deserve.

Ema Siddique, 28, deleted most of her social media accounts about five years ago after wondering if constant availability meant that her most important connections were not being tended to enough. When she learned of Carrier Pidge, she saw it as a natural extension of that mind-set.

Her pigeon was the one careening from London, where she lives, to a friend in Toronto (she messages another friend with the app who lives in Kuwait). Ms. Siddique and her friends don’t take the texts too seriously, but quickly began to use old-timey, “Bridgerton”-esque language, referring to one other as “my dearest lady.”

“It’s similar to a letter in the sense that you spend a lot of effort, and it does feel like every word that goes into it is intentional,” Ms. Siddique said.

She added: “You can track it, which adds to the excitement. I have one Carrier Pidge on the way from Kuwait, and you think, ‘What is she going to say in the next one?’”

item.title: Paramount and California to Hold Preliminary Talks on Warner Bros. Deal
item.description:
Representatives for Paramount and the State of California are set to meet on Monday to discuss a potential path for settling the state’s lawsuit that seeks to halt Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, four people briefed on the upcoming discussions said.

The talks are preliminary, and there is no assurance that they will lead to meaningful negotiations toward a settlement, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the discussions were private. Paramount requested the meeting, two of the people said.

Paramount’s merger with Warner Bros. would create a media powerhouse combining two major movie studios, multiple streaming services and the news outlets CNN and CBS News.

Last month, California led 12 state attorneys general in suing to block the deal, arguing it would create a media company with outsize market power in cable television and studios.

The meeting, which will include senior executives and lawyers from each side, has been in the works for a little over a week, said one of the people. It remains unclear what resolution Paramount might offer that would satisfy the attorneys general. Paramount declined to comment for this article.

California’s attorney general, Robert Bonta, has said he would be wiling to accept only structural remedies to resolve the lawsuit, which typically means selling off pieces of a business. Executives are often reluctant to hive off parts of a newly merged company because they have already made financial assumptions about the combined operations.

Paramount’s advisers have been evaluating possible solutions, one of the people said. Any solution would likely have to address at least one of two key concerns the states have: the size of Paramount’s cable business and the size of its movie studio businesses relative to their overall industries. A number of theater chains have come out in support of the deal in recent weeks.

“If the opposing party in litigation wants to meet in good faith to make a sincere effort to resolve the case, we’ll meet,” Mr. Bonta said Friday in a statement, adding that Paramount would need to make concessions to address the states’ concerns in any potential discussions. Variety earlier reported to the sides were planning to meet Monday.

With a trial scheduled for March, the delay could cost the company hundreds of millions of dollars in fees that the company must start paying to Warner Brothers shareholders if the deal is not closed by October. Paramount has agreed to pause the deal until June if the case has not been resolved by then.

The lawsuit has also delayed the cost savings that Paramount had been eyeing from the deal, while also creating great uncertainty for both companies, as well as the broader entertainment industry.

Concerns about the delay’s impact is contributing to mounting pressure for the two sides to come to a resolution. On Thursday, Mayor Karen Bass issued a release saying she was calling for “a swift and urgent resolution” to the litigation. She said the statement came on the heels of a meeting with labor leaders in the entertainment industry and members of the Mayor’s Entertainment Industry Council.

“Productions in LA are hurting and hard-working Angelenos are out of a job because ongoing disputes over the proposed merger have stalled filming in our city — it’s time for all parties to come to the table,” the mayor said in the release.

The Writers Guild Association, which has also sued to halt the acquisition, denounced Ms. Bass’s statement, saying it was “disappointed” that the mayor has chosen to “join Paramount’s pressure campaign” to settle the dispute.

David McCabe contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S. Economy Could Feel the Sting From Trade War With Canada
item.description:
Since President Trump has returned to office, the United States and Canada have repeatedly come close to an all-out trade war — only for Mr. Trump to dial back some of his harshest attacks against one of America’s closest allies.

But that period of relative calm came to an end on Saturday, as new 50 percent tariffs from Washington took effect, drawing a pointed threat from Canada to respond in kind. The resulting clash left the two North American neighbors barreling toward a dangerous tit-for-tat escalation, one that may yet inflict real harm on the U.S. economy.

For Mr. Trump, the return to trade brinkmanship reaffirmed a time-old truth: His tariffs are taxes on imports, meaning some of the cost of his latest duties may ultimately fall hardest on U.S. importers stung by years of persistently high prices.

Although Mr. Trump’s tariffs only cover a small subset of Canadian goods, the consequences could quickly spiral. If Canada retaliates, and Mr. Trump does the same, the result could be a series of new shocks for the U.S. economy at a time when it is already weathering plenty.

“The bigger deal is uncertainty,” said Scott Lincicome, the vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute.

Mr. Lincicome said that volatility had pervaded Mr. Trump’s entire second term, as his ever-shifting tariffs — raised and lowered sometimes by the stroke of a pen — roil Wall Street, anger the courts, infuriate U.S. allies and help to drive up the price of consumer goods domestically.

With Canada, though, Mr. Lincicome said the new clash could weigh heavily on businesses that transact across the U.S.-Canadian border. The retaliatory tariff increases could affect prices, and consequently translate to “slightly less investment, slightly less economic activity,” while the confusing trade climate persists.

In the end, Mr. Trump could still avert catastrophe and strike a deal with Canada as soon as this weekend. But, by Saturday morning, that appeared unlikely: Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, told Fox News that there were no new talks planned with his Canadian counterparts, adding that the administration was “moving forward” with its tariffs.

In response, Canada showed no sign that it planned to back down. Hours later, Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, threatened to unveil its own tariff measures against the United States shortly after Labor Day, targeting sectors including agriculture, steel and electronics.

At one point, Mr. Carney even said his country was “at war.”

Mr. Trump’s new duties — set at 50 percent — apply to about $20 billion in Canada’s exports to the United States, according to administration officials. The list of covered goods numbers into the hundreds, and includes Canadian-made hockey sticks, furniture and dairy products, which could become too expensive for U.S. consumers to import.

Overall, though, the tariffs apply to a small fraction of trade between the two nations, muting the impact, at least for now. In an early analysis, John Ricco, the deputy director of policy analysis at the Yale Budget Lab, a nonpartisan think tank, said the new tariffs would raise the average tariff rate on Canadian imports to about 7.6 percent, from roughly 5.3 percent.

The United States already had in place steep tariffs on other critical Canadian imports, including its lumber, steel and cars. But, unlike Mr. Trump’s past tariffs, the duties he imposed Saturday come with no special exemption for goods that are otherwise covered under a trade agreement the United States brokered with Canada and Mexico, a pact that the president separately has said he hopes to revise or kill.

Joe Brusuelas, the chief economist at the audit and consulting firm RSM US, said he still believed a deal was possible. But he added that the risks of escalation were also real — and could be costly.

For one thing, Mr. Brusuelas said he expected that Canada might take aim “where it hurts the most,” perhaps including the U.S. auto industry. That could result in “risks around the inflation outlook” at a time when manufacturing continues to lag.

A retaliatory cycle could complicate the nation’s existing battle with inflation, which remains well above the 2 percent target that the Federal Reserve aims for, despite Mr. Trump’s arguments to the contrary. In fact, rising prices prompted the president just this week to relax his tariffs on beef imports, a tacit acknowledgment that his trade policies had hit Americans’ wallets.

Increasingly, those economic anxieties have also spilled into financial markets. Concerns about America’s mounting debt load, which hit $40 trillion this week, helped send yields on government bonds soaring. The war with Iran has also posed economic challenges, crimping growth globally while causing fuel costs to rise.

Some Democrats in Congress cited additional risks as they attacked the president in recent days, arguing that his threats against Canada could create real economic blowback for the United States. Shortly after the tariffs went into effect, Senator Peter Welch, Democrat of Vermont, described the duties as a “slap in the face” to farmers and others in his state that do business across the border.

“Cross-border business relationships, built over decades, are in the lurch,” he said. “Uncertainty about a long-term trade deal with our closest ally has grown, and long-term trade negotiations seem to now be on ice.”

But there was still a sense among some on Washington and Wall Street that the worst with Canada might still be avoided — and that the drama playing out in public reflected the now-usual course of business with Mr. Trump.

“We’ve all been conditioned to the sequencing of these negotiations,” Mr. Brusuelas said.
